email.scenario: You recently returned a projector you rented for a client presentation, and the invoice emailed to you afterward lists a late fee under a rental order number that isn't yours. You need a corrected receipt before your workplace's expense report deadline this Friday.
email.subject: Incorrect Late Fee on Invoice #48219
bullets: Explain that the invoice lists a late fee under the wrong rental order number.
Ask why the charge was applied to your account and whether the projector's return was logged correctly.
Suggest that the company issue a corrected receipt before your expense report deadline.

academicDiscussion.professorPost: Many museums are considering removing the printed wall labels beside artworks and requiring visitors to use a smartphone app instead to read curatorial information. Supporters say this creates a cleaner, more immersive gallery space, while others worry about visitors who don't own or want to use a smartphone. Should galleries remove the printed labels and require an app instead? Why or why not?

studentPosts.name: Maya
studentPosts.post: I don't think galleries should remove the printed labels. Not every visitor owns a smartphone, and some don't want to use one while they're trying to relax and look at art. Printed labels let anyone glance at the information immediately without opening an app or worrying about a dead battery.

studentPosts.name: Theo
studentPosts.post: I disagree with Maya. Printed labels clutter the walls and pull attention away from the artwork itself. Most visitors already carry a phone, and an app can offer more than a small placard ever could, including enlarged images, audio narration, and translations that a paper label just can't fit.
